primitives.name: Dribble Hand-Off Classification
primitives.verbatim_quote: One of the most effective actions in dynamic offensive strategies in basketball is the dribble hand-off (DHO).
primitives.assumptions: Player trajectories are captured via SportVU tracking data; DHOs involve coordinated movement of two offensive players.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When player coordination fails or intent is obscured by fake actions.

layer2.mapping: DHO variants are isomorphic to trajectory path clusters in hexbin space, enabling ML classification via geometric similarity.

primitives.name: Hexbin Trajectory Encoding
primitives.verbatim_quote: This pipeline consists of a combination of player tracking data and event labels, a rule set to identify candidate actions, player trajectories embedded into hexbin cell paths, and passing the completed training set of generated features to the classification and clustering models.
primitives.assumptions: Player movement data is discretized into hexagonal bins for spatial feature extraction.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When spatial resolution is insufficient to distinguish fine-grained motion.

layer2.mapping: Hexbin encoding serves as kernel for embedding continuous player paths into discrete topological features.
layer2.telemetry: Occupancy counts per hexbin cell and path traversal frequency.

The core mathematical structure underlying DHO classification lies in the topological embedding of player trajectories into a hexagonal grid system. Each player's movement path is projected onto a hexbin lattice, where each bin represents a spatial region. The resulting sequence of occupied bins forms a discrete path that encodes both spatial and temporal dynamics. These paths are then fed into a classification pipeline that uses supervised learning to distinguish between standard and fake DHOs. The key insight is that the geometric properties of these hexbin paths—such as path length, curvature, and occupancy density—are invariant under translation and rotation, making them robust features for machine learning models. The failure mode arises when the hexbin resolution is too coarse to differentiate subtle variations in movement, or when the DHO is intentionally disguised to mimic other actions. The dual nature of DHOs—both as a strategic tool and a potential deception—requires a probabilistic model that accounts for uncertainty in player intent. This leads to a Bayesian framework where prior beliefs about action type are updated based on observed trajectory features.
